Classify the following amines as primary, secondary or tertiary:
(i) \(\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_7-\text{NH}_2\) (naphthalene carrying the \(-\text{NH}_2\) group at position 1)
(ii) \(\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_7-\text{N}(\text{CH}_3)_2\) (naphthalene carrying the \(-\text{N}(\text{CH}_3)_2\) group at position 1)
(iii) \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{CHNH}_2\)
(iv) \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\)
_note: Parts (i) and (ii) are printed as drawn naphthalene ring structures (substituent on the carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, i.e. position 1). They are transcribed here as condensed formulae plus a positional description, which is lossless for this question — the classification turns only on the substituent borne by nitrogen.

Write chemical equations for the following reactions:
(i) Reaction of ethanolic \(\text{NH}_3\) with \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}\).
(ii) Ammonolysis of benzyl chloride and reaction of amine so formed with two moles of \(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}\).
solution:
(i) Successive alkylation of ammonia by chloroethane:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5-\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{NH}_3} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5-\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}} (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH} \xrightarrow{\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}} (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{N} \xrightarrow{\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}} (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_4\overset{+}{\text{N}}\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}}\)
Chloroethane \(\rightarrow\) Ethanamine \(\rightarrow\) N-Ethylethanamine \(\rightarrow\) N,N-Diethylethanamine \(\rightarrow\) Quaternary ammonium salt.

(ii) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{NH}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{2\,\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{N}(\text{CH}_3)_2\)
Benzyl chloride \(\rightarrow\) Benzylamine \(\rightarrow\) N,N-Dimethylphenylmethanamine.

stem:
Write chemical equations for the following conversions:
(i) \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}\) into \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2\)
(ii) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}\) into \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2\)
solution:
Both conversions add one carbon, so the halide is first converted to a nitrile and the nitrile is then reduced.

(i) \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{Ethanolic NaCN}} \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{C} \equiv \text{N} \xrightarrow{\text{reduction}} \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2\)
Chloroethane \(\rightarrow\) Propanenitrile \(\rightarrow\) Propan-1-amine.

(ii) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{Ethanolic NaCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{C} \equiv \text{N} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2\)
Chlorophenylmethane (benzyl chloride) \(\rightarrow\) Phenylethanenitrile (benzyl cyanide) \(\rightarrow\) 2-Phenylethanamine.

stem:
Write structures and IUPAC names of
(i) the amide which gives propanamine by Hoffmann bromamide reaction.
(ii) the amine produced by the Hoffmann degradation of benzamide.
solution:
In the Hoffmann bromamide degradation the amine formed has one carbon less than the amide.

(i) Propanamine contains three carbons. Hence the amide molecule must contain four carbon atoms:
\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CONH}_2\), Butanamide.

(ii) Benzamide is an aromatic amide containing seven carbon atoms. Hence the amine formed is an aromatic primary amine containing six carbon atoms:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{NH}_2\), Aniline or benzenamine.
_note: The book prints the name as "Hoffmann" (double f) in the chapter body and in this Example, but as "Hofmann's" (single f) in Exercise 9.7(iii). Transcribed as printed in each place.

subtopic: Importance of Diazonium Salts in Synthesis of Aromatic Compounds
stem: How will you convert 4-nitrotoluene to 2-bromobenzoic acid?
solution:
\(\text{4-Nitrotoluene} \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2} \text{2-Bromo-4-nitrotoluene} \xrightarrow{\text{Sn/HCl}} \text{3-Bromo-4-methylaniline}\)
\(\xrightarrow[273-278\ \text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{the corresponding diazonium chloride} \xrightarrow[\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2]{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{2-Bromotoluene} \xrightarrow[\overset{-}{\text{O}}\text{H}]{\text{KMnO}_4} \text{2-Bromobenzoic acid}\)
Bromination of 4-nitrotoluene puts bromine ortho to the methyl group (the \(-\text{CH}_3\) group is o-/p- directing and the \(-\text{NO}_2\) group is m- directing, and both send the electrophile to the same position). The nitro group is then reduced to \(-\text{NH}_2\) with Sn/HCl, diazotised at 273-278 K, and the diazonium group is replaced by hydrogen using hypophosphorous acid. Finally the methyl group is oxidised to \(-\text{COOH}\) with alkaline \(\text{KMnO}_4\), giving 2-bromobenzoic acid.

(i) Methylamine and dimethylamine
(ii) Secondary and tertiary amines
(iii) Ethylamine and aniline
(iv) Aniline and benzylamine
(v) Aniline and N-methylaniline.

Account for the following:
(i) \(\text{p}K_b\) of aniline is more than that of methylamine.
(ii) Ethylamine is soluble in water whereas aniline is not.
(iii) Methylamine in water reacts with ferric chloride to precipitate hydrated ferric oxide.
(iv) Although amino group is \(o-\) and \(p-\) directing in aromatic electrophilic substitution reactions, aniline on nitration gives a substantial amount of \(m\)-nitroaniline.
(v) Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
(vi) Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are more stable than those of aliphatic amines.
(vii) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is preferred for synthesising primary amines.

Arrange the following:
(i) In decreasing order of the \(\text{p}K_b\) values:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\), \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_3\), \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\) and \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\)
(ii) In increasing order of basic strength:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\), \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}(\text{CH}_3)_2\), \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\) and \(\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2\)
(iii) In increasing order of basic strength:
(a) Aniline, \(p\)-nitroaniline and \(p\)-toluidine
(b) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\), \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_3\), \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\).
(iv) In decreasing order of basic strength in gas phase:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\), \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\), \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{N}\) and \(\text{NH}_3\)
(v) In increasing order of boiling point:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\), \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH}\), \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\)
(vi) In increasing order of solubility in water:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\), \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\), \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\).
